questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The best diets to follow after the Christmas holidays
Where the attitudes behind fat-shaming come from
How doctors measure body fat in their patients
Why most New Year's resolutions usually fail
questions.why: Neil says they will be asking where the attitudes behind fat-shaming come from.

questions.q: Why do Neil and Georgina both want to lose weight?
options: Their doctors told them to lose weight for their health
They are training together for a charity run
They put on weight in lockdown and at Christmas
They want to look good for a New Year's party
questions.why: Georgina ate a lot of chocolate at Christmas, and Neil gained weight in lockdown and then over Christmas.

questions.q: According to Professor Saguy, why did doctors start using the term 'obesity'?
options: To show it was a medical issue they were experts in
To make overweight people feel ashamed of their size
To replace an older word that sounded rude to patients
To help drug companies sell new weight-loss medicines
questions.why: She says doctors wanted to say it was a medical issue over which they had authority and expertise.

questions.q: How has the meaning of 'obese' changed over time, according to Neil?
options: It now only describes children who are overweight
It has become a more polite and neutral word
It is no longer used by doctors or scientists
It has become a term of discrimination and abuse
questions.why: Neil says it began as an individual medical problem but has become a term of discrimination and abuse.

questions.q: What are Harvard's implicit bias tests most famous for revealing?
options: Prejudice about age
Racial prejudice
Prejudice about weight
Prejudice about wealth
questions.why: Georgina says the tests are most famous for revealing racial prejudice, though they also measure weight bias.

questions.q: According to Professor Crandall, what do many westerners believe about fat people?
options: They are usually happier and more relaxed than others
Their weight is mostly caused by a medical illness
They cannot find or afford healthy food nearby
They are lazy and to blame for their condition
questions.why: He says people see fatness as a sign of laziness and 'a thing that you do to yourself'.

questions.q: What does Neil say about what really determines a person's weight?
options: Environment and genetics matter, up to 80%
It depends only on how much exercise you do
It depends only on what and how much you eat
Genetics have almost no effect on body size
questions.why: Neil says weight is also determined by environment and genetics, up to 80% in some cases.

questions.q: What is Georgina's view of fat-shaming?
options: It works well as long as it is done kindly
It is only really a problem on social media
It is not a good way to help people lose weight
It is much less common than most people think
questions.why: She says that even if weight were under personal control, fat-shaming doesn't seem the right way to help.
